title: Returns, volatility and drawdown from a CSV
objectives: Build the 1.1 exit project: one script from a price file to three charts
Compute annualised volatility and maximum drawdown and show them honestly

screens.title: The worst fall, by eye
screens.prose: The exit project starts from a file of daily closes, `prices.csv`, and ends with three charts: returns, volatility and drawdown. First, find the drawdown by eye.
screens.question: Tap the close where the deepest fall begins and the close where it ends.

hints.text: A fall begins at a peak: the highest close so far.
The highest close is £54.00 on 6 March.
From £54.00 the price falls for two days, to £48.60 on 8 March.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at a peak and follow the fall to its lowest close.

byKey.next-day: The fall carries on past 7 March. 8 March is lower still, at £48.60.
byKey.first: The fall starts at the peak, £54.00, not at the first close.

explain.text: You started at the peak and followed the fall to its lowest close: $48.60 / 54.00 - 1 = -0.10$. That is the maximum drawdown, the number our script must find for itself.

hints.text: Which step needs every other step done first?

Read, sort, returns, volatility, draw, save.

feedback.correct: Each step uses only what the steps before it made.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each step needs before it can run.

byKey.sort: Sorting needs rows to sort, so reading comes first.
byKey.ret: Returns on unsorted rows run backwards in time. Sort before you compute.
byKey.save: You can only save a figure once it is drawn.

widget.solution:
import csv
import io


def load_closes(text):
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)))
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["date"])
    return [float(r["close"]) for r in rows]

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: the second file arrives newest first.

explain.text: Sorting the dictionaries by their date text puts them in time order, because ISO dates sort like numbers. `float` turns `"48.60"` into 48.6, ready for returns.

screens.title: From daily to annual
screens.prose: Daily returns have a standard deviation. Volatility is quoted per year. With about 252 trading days a year, it scales by $\sqrt{252}$, not 252, because independent variances add.
screens.question: A stock's daily returns have a standard deviation of 1.20%. What is its annualised volatility, in %?

hints.text: Variances add over days; standard deviations do not.
A year's variance is 252 daily variances, so its standard deviation is √252 daily ones.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by the square root of 252.

byKey.times: You multiplied by 252. Variances add over days, so the standard deviation grows with √252.
byKey.months: That uses √12, for monthly returns. These returns are daily.
byKey.same: That is the daily figure. Volatility is quoted per year.

explain.text: Over 252 independent days the variance is $252\sigma^2$, so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{252}\,\sigma = 15.87 \times 1.20\% = 19.05\%$.

widget.solution:
import math
import statistics


def summary(closes):
    rets = [closes[i] / closes[i - 1] - 1 for i in range(1, len(closes))]
    vol = statistics.stdev(rets) * math.sqrt(252)
    peak, mdd = closes[0], 0.0
    for p in closes:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        mdd = min(mdd, p / peak - 1)
    return [round(vol, 4), round(mdd, 4)]
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests, each rounded to 4 places. No matplotlib here, so it runs quickly.

For the drawdown, carry the highest close so far through a loop.
In the loop: `peak = max(peak, p)`, then `mdd = min(mdd, p / peak - 1)`, starting from `mdd = 0.0`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: the second one hides its lowest close before its peak.

explain.text: The running peak only ever rises, so each drawdown compares a close with the best close before it. The third test never falls, so its drawdown is exactly 0.

screens.title: Highest and lowest
screens.prose: A second stock. A colleague computes its maximum drawdown as the gap between its highest and lowest close: $(60.00 - 40.00) / 60.00$.
screens.question: What is the stock's true maximum drawdown?

options.why: You took the highest and lowest closes. The £40.00 came before the £60.00 peak, so no one who held it lost that.
That is the £20 gap over the low, £40.00. The low came first, so it is not a fall at all.
That is one day's fall, £57.00 to £54.00. Measure from the peak, £60.00.

hints.text: A drawdown is a fall from a peak that came before it.
The lowest close, £40.00, is the very first one.
After the £60.00 peak the lowest close is £54.00: $54.00 / 60.00 - 1 = -0.10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only a low after the peak counts.

byKey.range: You used the highest and lowest closes, ignoring their order. The £40.00 came first, before any peak. The real worst fall is £60.00 to £54.00: −10%.

explain.text: Order matters: a drawdown runs from a peak to a later low, here £60.00 to £54.00, or −10.00%. The low of £40.00 came first and the price rose from it. That is why `summary` tracks the running peak, the best close so far.

screens.title: Maximum drawdown, line by line
screens.prose: Your loop computed the maximum drawdown in three moves. Write each as a formula, with $p_t$ the close on day $t$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $M_t = \max(p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_t)$, the running peak: the best close so far
$D_t = p_t / M_t - 1$, today's drawdown, 0 at a new peak
$\text{MDD} = \min_t D_t$, the deepest drawdown over the whole history

hints.text: Which quantity does each line need from the line before?
$D_t$ divides by $M_t$, so $M_t$ comes first.
Peak, then drawdown, then the minimum of the drawdowns.

feedback.correct: Peak, drawdown, then the worst drawdown.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one above it.

byKey.d: $D_t$ divides by $M_t$, so the running peak must be defined first.
byKey.mdd: The minimum is taken over drawdowns, so they must exist first.

explain.text: For the trap's stock, $M_t$ reaches £60.00 on 6 May and stays there. $D_t$ is then 0, −5%, −10% and −3.3%, so the MDD is −10%. The early £40.00 never enters, since $M_0 = p_0$ gives $D_0 = 0$.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math
import statistics


def returns(closes):
    return [closes[i] / closes[i - 1] - 1 for i in range(1, len(closes))]


def rolling_vol(rets, n=5):
    # (days, vols): annualised volatility of the n returns ending on each day
    days = list(range(n, len(rets) + 1))
    vols = [statistics.stdev(rets[d - n:d]) * math.sqrt(252) for d in days]
    return days, vols


def drawdown(closes):
    peak, out = closes[0], []
    for p in closes:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        out.append(p / peak - 1)
    return out


def exit_figure(closes):
    rets = returns(closes)
    days, vols = rolling_vol(rets)
    dd = drawdown(closes)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(8, 7))
    axes[0].plot(range(1, len(closes)), rets)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("Daily return")
    axes[1].plot(days, vols)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("Volatility, annualised")
    axes[2].plot(range(len(closes)), dd)
    axes[2].set_ylabel("Drawdown")
    mdd = min(dd)
    t = dd.index(mdd)
    axes[2].annotate(f"Max drawdown {mdd:.1%}", xy=(t, mdd))
    fig.savefig("exit.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    return fig, axes

examples.setup: import os; plt.close("all"); fig, axes = exit_figure([50.0, 52.0, 51.0, 54.0, 49.5, 48.6, 50.4, 53.1])

quiz.question: What goes wrong?

Python raises an error on unsorted dates

options.text: Only the volatility is wrong; the drawdown is fine
options.why: The drawdown needs time order too: the running peak would run backwards.

options.why: A return compares a close with the one before it in time. Reversed rows reverse that.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what “the close before” means on reversed rows.

explain.text: On reversed rows, "the row above" is tomorrow, so every return and every running peak runs backwards. No error appears, which is why the sort comes right after reading.
